newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel and PLO seal Hebron agreement.
newsitem.headline: Israel and PLO seal Hebron agreement.

text.p: Israel will hand over most of Hebron to Palestinian rule within 10 days under a long-elusive agreement concluded with the PLO on Wednesday, officials said.

Negotiators initialled the deal behind closed doors on the border between Israel and the Gaza Strip at a late-night summit between Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Palestinian President Yasser Arafat.

U.S. President Bill Clinton, whose special envoy Dennis Ross mediated between the two sides during months of arduous talks, hailed the deal as a contribution to a "lasting and secure Middle East peace".
Israel's cabinet and the Palestinian Authority will meet separately later on Wednesday to approve the deal.
"The agreement has been signed a few minutes ago by (negotiators) Dan Shomron and Saeb Erekat," Netanyahu's spokesman Shai Bazak told reporters at the Erez crossing.

Chief Palestinian negotiator Mahmoud Abbas told Reuters the deal requires Israel to withdraw its troops from 80 percent of Hebron within 10 days and implement the first of three subsequent West Bank redeployments by March 7.

"We are glad we have finalised the Hebron deal. It is the first agreement we have signed with the Likud. We hope this will be the beginning of more deals with this governement," said Abbas, better known as Abu Mazen.
Other PLO officials said a formal ceremony would be held on Friday with European, Arab and American participation.
Ross, who has tugged relentessly since October to bring the two sides together, was visibly relieved after negotiators initialled the deal.
"I am very pleased to announce on behalf of the two leaders that they have reached an agreement," Ross told reporters as Netanyahu and Arafat emerged from their negotiations.
Netanyahu and Arafat shook hands but did not speak to reporters.
Ross said the agreement included a "note for the record" which dealt with future Israeli redeployments from the West Bank and other non-Hebron related issues.

"These two documents represent a very important building block in terms of developing the relations between the two sides and in terms of laying out a pathway of greater hope and the possibility for peace in the Middle East," he said.
Palestitnian officials said the United States provided a letter assuring it would help "advance implementation of the interim agreement".
They said Israelis and Palestinians spelled out commitments to each other in another section of the agreement titled "Agreed Minutes" but refused to disclose its contents.
Bazak said Israel had secured a Palestinian commitment to hand over Palestinian guerrillas who attacked Israelis.

"The American letter of assurance...will say unequivocally that the Palestinian Authority promises to hand over suspects and extradite murderers to Israel according to their commitments in the Oslo accords," he told reporters.
After the deal was concluded, Netanyahu and Arafat spoke by phone with Clinton, Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak and Jordan's King Hussein, Bazak said.

Hebron, a West Bank flashpoint, is home to 400 militant Jewish settlers and 100,000 Arabs. It was due to be given self-rule 10 months ago but violence, security concerns and Israel's change of government in June delayed the pullback.
By sealing the Hebron deal Netanyahu did what he and his right-wing Likud party said they would never do -- cede part of the biblical Land of Israel to Palestinians.
In Jerusalem, nearly 200 settler leaders who oppose the Hebron deal called on members of Netanyahu's cabinet to vote against it.
"This is a dark day for Jews in the Land of Israel," said Hebron settler Moshe Ben Zimra. "The agreement signed today will lead to a massacre of Jews in Hebron," he told Israel Radio.
At least seven of 18 cabinet members have said they will oppose the agreement when it comes up for government approval.
"Tomorrow (on Wednesday) at around noon the cabinet will meet and I am sure they will approve the Hebron agreement by a majority," Bazak told reporters.
